To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

women who had a high number of psychosocia l problems were at higher risk for HIV and STDs, had less knowledge about HIV and STDs and had less educational attainment, and were less likely to complete the HIV and STD prevention intervention

(a) women at risk for HIV/STD who have more psychosocial problems are more likely to be African-American and have lower education and knowledge about HIV/ STD; (b) women with more psychosocial difficulties are less likely to attend an HIV/STD intervention and have lower risk; and (c) women with more problems are less likely to be retained in an HIV/ STD intervention.
women who were experiencing more psychosocial problems were less likely to complete a group intervention for HIV/STD prevention.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of psychosocial factors in women’s attrition from an intervention to reduce HIV/STD risk.
the development and evaluation of effective interventions to reduce the risk of HIV/STD infection and other adverse health outcomes in high risk women.
the influence of psychosociological difficulties on women's retention in HIV prevention programs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
psychosocial factors are important to consider in the design of interventions, but that there are many other important factors to consider as well.
psychosocial problems are a barrier to women's attendance at HIV/STD prevention interventions.
the psychosocial problems of the participants were the main reason for attrition in the HIV prevention group counselling program.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
women at high HIV/STD risk are likely to have a range of psychosocial and structural difficulties.
the women who had the greatest need for the intervention were also those least likely to benefit from it.
the women who are most in need of intervention are least likely to attend, and that we need to develop interventions that can be delivered to them.
The main takeaway from our work is that
women with multiple psychosocial problems may be less likely to attend HIV/STD prevention interventions, even when the programs are designed to address their specific needs.
women’s psychosocial difficulties may influence their attendance in HIV/STD risk reduction programs.
the psychosocial problems experienced by the distressed group are likely related to HIV/STD risk and should be addressed by interventionists.
